A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MokA and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. All 15 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2 support comparison, including matching relocated appendix material.

before.justification: v1 reports original multimodal benchmark experiments, component ablations, partial-modality inference tests, efficiency measurements, and attention visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds four-modality evaluation, expanded efficiency measurements, and audio–visual attention and rank ablations.

M1.justification: Equations (7)–(13) introduce modality-specific coefficients λa and λv controlling attention contributions, generalizing v1's unit-weight additions. The modality-specific A matrices, shared B matrix, and attention mechanism remain intact. The PDFs do not establish which coefficient values produced the retained experimental results.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds evaluation on MCUB-3 with audio, visual, point-cloud, and language inputs. This substantively extends coverage beyond the original two- and three-modality scenarios by introducing point-cloud data and a four-modality setting. Existing training datasets and evaluation benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the retained benchmark tables are unchanged. New Table 9 adds comparisons against MokA variants with audio-query and video-query audio–visual attention. The MCUB-3 comparison uses the existing LoRA baseline rather than introducing another external comparator.

E3.justification: Table 6 replaces the reported inference-latency metric with average forward time per sample. Appendix D adds normalized FLOPs and GPU-memory measurements, while Appendix F evaluates ranks 4, 8, and 12. The original training recipe remains unchanged; the PDFs do not establish comparable timing procedures across versions.

E4.justification: Appendices E and F add targeted tests of additional audio–visual attention and sensitivity to rank. Appendix D expands resource-cost analysis across two-, three-, and four-modality settings. Existing component ablations, interaction variants, linear-projection experiments, and attention case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added results retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantive results for four-modality evaluation and resource costs: MCUB-3 accuracy is 37.41% for LoRA versus 45.58% for MokA, and Table 8 reports MokA forward-time ratios of 1.069, 1.134, and 1.213 across the three modality settings. Tables 9–10 add attention-variant and rank results. Table 6 replaces latency ratios of 1.36/1.13 for Multiple LoRA/MokA with forward-time ratios of 1.006/1.069; these are not established same-setting speedups. Other retained tables preserve their scores.

T1.justification: Equations (7)–(13) revise the formal update and its unimodal/cross-modal decomposition to include λa- and λv-weighted attention residuals. This generalizes the mathematical definition beyond v1's unit coefficients. No new assumptions, theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding discussion retain the same central contribution: modality-specific compression and explicit cross-modal interaction enable effective multimodal adaptation. The additional experiments support this existing claim without redefining the main contribution or novelty claim.

C2.justification: New appendix discussion interprets the four-modality result as evidence of scalability, attributes additional computation to cross-attention, and concludes that further audio–visual interaction offers limited benefits. Existing mechanism explanations and broader-impact qualifications are retained, including the relocated case-study and impact sections.

D1.justification: v2 identifies λa and λv as attention-strength hyperparameters and specifies ranks and the LLaMA2 backbone for added ablations. Existing implementation and project-access information remains unchanged. Numerical λ settings, point-cloud branch implementation, and hardware or timing procedures for the expanded efficiency evaluation are not supplied.

R1.justification: v2 adds three cited works: Model Composition for Multimodal Large Language Models, CMSL: Cross-Modal Style Learning for Few-Shot Image Generation, and Large-Scale Multi-Modal Pre-Trained Models: A Comprehensive Survey. These support the new benchmark and background discussion; the positioning relative to LoRA and multimodal adaptation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 adds four appendix sections and acknowledgements, updates affiliation/contact and conference text, and changes the Figure 1 experiment description from first generation step to prefilling stage. Existing appendix sections are relabeled rather than removed.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–10 and changes Table 6's timing header and layout. The original linear-projection Table 8 becomes Table 11 and moves away from its discussion. All six figures are retained, with limited caption and formatting changes rather than substantive redraws.

improvement.justification: The four-modality experiment, rank controls, audio–visual attention ablations, and expanded cost measurements provide useful additional support for MokA's applicability and design choices. The gain is limited by missing scaling-coefficient values and implementation details for the new setting, plus an unexplained timing-metric replacement while surrounding prose still discusses inference latency. The core evidence and contribution otherwise remain stable.
